justice: Most of the street space is allocated to motor vehicles, with trucks parked on both sides and only a narrow or unclear pedestrian zone visible.
No dedicated bicycle lane, protected shoulder, or marked pedestrian facility is visible, suggesting uneven distribution of space among walking, cycling, and driving users.
Accessibility is limited because there are no visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked crossings connecting the roadside edges.
The gravel-paver edge and unbuffered roadside parking create a less usable margin for non-motorized users compared with the paved carriageway reserved for vehicles.
safety: Several trucks and small vehicles are parked directly along the road edge, narrowing the effective travel space and increasing conflict risk for all users.
There is no visible sidewalk separation, guardrail, or curb buffer between moving traffic and potential pedestrians.
The curved roadway ahead reduces sightlines, especially with large blue trucks partially blocking views near the bend.
No marked crosswalks, traffic-calming devices, or clear warning markings are visible in the scene.
livability: The area appears auto- and freight-oriented, with multiple parked trucks dominating the frontage rather than active public street life.
There are trees and green landscape areas on the left, but they function more as setback greenery than as usable public social space.
No benches, kiosks, café seating, or visible pedestrian gathering amenities are present along the street edge.
The street lacks signs of everyday pedestrian activity, which weakens the sense of neighborhood vitality.
sustainability: Some trees and planted greenery are present along the left side and in the background, providing limited ecological value.
The absence of visible bike lanes, bus stop infrastructure, or strong transit priority reduces support for low-carbon travel choices.
Large utility lines and a road environment dominated by parked trucks suggest a transport pattern centered on motorized freight.
Permeable paving appears on the roadside parking/edge areas, which may slightly help stormwater infiltration compared with fully sealed surfaces.
aesthetics: The scene has a somewhat open green backdrop, but the visual quality is weakened by multiple parked trucks and utility wires overhead.
Large power lines, poles, and cable bundles create visual clutter across the sky.
The roadside surface transitions from asphalt to rough gravel/permeable blocks, giving the corridor a utilitarian and unfinished appearance.
Street trees are present but sparse and heavily pruned, so they contribute limited canopy and limited visual softness.
comfort: Thermal comfort is weak because tree canopies are small and provide very little shade over the road or roadside walking areas.
Physical comfort is low due to the absence of clear sidewalks, benches, and dedicated waiting or resting spaces.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the dominance of trucks and open roadside parking, which can make the environment feel exposed and vehicle-prioritized.
The road surface appears relatively even for vehicles, but the side margins look rougher and less comfortable for walking or standing.
walkability: There is no clearly marked continuous sidewalk visible along either side of the road.
Parked trucks occupy the road edges, forcing any pedestrian movement closer to vehicular space.
No zebra crossing, pedestrian signal, or curb extension is visible to support safe crossing or route continuity.
Limited shade from the small pruned trees reduces walking attractiveness and thermal comfort.
bikeability: No bike lane, painted shoulder, or protected cycling facility is visible anywhere on the roadway.
Parked trucks along both sides create dooring, merging, and visibility hazards for cyclists.
The narrow effective carriageway and curve ahead increase conflict risk between bicycles and motor vehicles.
No bicycle parking, bike markings, or intersection treatments are present to support cycling use.
